3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

5	A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.
6	
7	A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.
8	
9	The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.
10	
11	To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.
12	
13	The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

content.content:
1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
42	
43	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
44	
45	An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.
46	
47	Operation
48	
49	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
50	
51	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
52	
53	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
54	
55	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
56

The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

content.content:
1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

lines: The latch and the force-limiting drive train

-FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

+The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

+FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so that the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints is shown schematically.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The region within the inner boundary is open, the ring being shown removed from the frame.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those circumferential positions, and the passage of each opening through the annulus, are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary; that handedness, and the corresponding sense of ring rotation, are shown schematically.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs as a short straight surface slanting inward toward that joint, the ring drive face 36. Which segment carries it, and its position on the outer boundary, are shown schematically.

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line acting between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body so as to urge the jaw carriage 30 upward, that is, radially outward; its line of action is shown schematically. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp in the closed condition, parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the joint surfaces, the narrow gap between the two frame ends and the projection of the band ends into it, the handle mounting and its gap, and the opening for the indicator pin 56; the wedge 52 advance direction; and the force-limiting spring stack 54 as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a further band of like width from the right. A narrow radial gap separates the two bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces facing one another circumferentially, in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a short straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right. A short arm reaches from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack, and the lever runs up and right through a gap between the top and right walls, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the annular frame body and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from the frame. The latch 16 is drawn in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude there is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of that body and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; these positions are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the outer surface of the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies wholly in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its upper end is a short distance above the outer boundary of the annular frame body and its lower end is at the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage, where that face meets the pipe 90, so the line stops at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points to the same side of the line. That line is the cutting plane of the sectional view of FIG. 3, and the two arrows give the direction in which that section is viewed.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the annular frame body at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44 and its seats, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A narrow rectangular opening runs into the block from its left face and closes within the block toward the right. That opening is the oblique slot 34. It lies in the lower portion of the block, leaving a broad hatched region of the block above it and hatched material below it and right of its closed end. Its depth is shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging the jaw carriage 30 upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp in the closed condition, parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the joint surfaces, the gap between the two frame ends and the projection of the band ends into it, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening through which it passes, the hole for the indicator pin 56, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the two bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces facing one another, in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a short straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

The latch handle 50 is a plain elongated lever of constant width, its two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between those edges plain. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, and a short arm reaches from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44 and its seats, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A narrow rectangular opening runs into the block from its left face and closes within the block toward the right. That opening is the oblique slot 34. It lies in the lower portion of the block, leaving a broad hatched region of the block above it and hatched material below it and right of its closed end. Its depth is shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging the jaw carriage 30 upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the lowest body.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp in the closed condition, parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the joint surfaces, the gap between the two frame ends and the projection of the band ends into it, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening through which it passes, the hole for the indicator pin 56, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the two bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces facing one another, in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a short straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

The latch handle 50 is a plain elongated lever of constant width, its two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between those edges plain. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, and a short arm reaches from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically, from the top of the view to the bottom, and the radial direction runs horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view shows only the two frame ends at this joint and the ends of the two cam ring segments carried there. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region shown, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, the width of the gap, and how far each segment end reaches into it.

Two bodies stand one above the other, one occupying the upper part of the view and the other the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap running across the middle of the view between them.

Each body is an upright strip bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by a second arc concentric with it, both arcs running the height of that body. The upper body ends downward at a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left boundary to its right, and the lower body ends upward at a like horizontal end face, the two faces meeting the gap from above and from below. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body, spaced inward from both of its arcuate boundaries, lies an upright block drawn in outline whose lower end reaches down into the gap. That block is the first cam ring segment 22. Within the lower body lies a like upright block, spaced inward from both of its boundaries, whose upper end reaches up into the gap. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

In the gap the lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The two frame bodies carry section hatching at the broken-away near wall and the two cam ring segments are drawn in outline, so each segment reads as a separate body carried by its own frame half.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp in the closed condition, parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the gap between the two frame ends, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening through which it passes, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the two bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces facing one another, in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a short straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

The latch handle 50 is a plain elongated lever of constant width, its two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between those edges plain. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, and a short arm reaches from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

input.summary: Repaired all five failing drawing sheets by correcting the figure briefs, without touching the claims, the detailed description, the drawing descriptions, or the numeral table. FIG. 1's cutting-plane line is now bounded so it cannot run the full diameter; FIG. 2 assigns the ring drive face unambiguously to the second cam ring segment and states that the first segment's outer boundary is circular; FIG. 3 gives the segmented cam ring and the oblique slot widely separated anchor regions by placing the slot in the lower portion of the block and anchoring the ring in the broad hatched region above it; FIG. 4 describes the latch handle positively as a plain constant-width lever with two unbroken long edges and a plain area between them, and describes the housing opening as a positive gap between the top and right walls rather than a "handle mounting and its gap"; FIG. 6 restates the view so the circumferential direction runs vertically, the two frame ends stand one above the other, and the joint gap is a horizontal band across the middle. Every brief that grew was trimmed back under the 2800-character limit by removing hedges and wordiness, not by dropping required geometry. All 26 numerals, the per-sheet numeral lists, and the sheet assignments are unchanged, so figure coverage is intact.
reasoning: FIG. 1: the old brief said the line extends 'past the outer boundary at one end and past the jaw pad at the other', and 'past the jaw pad' invited the renderer to carry it across the pipe and out the far side. The line is now bounded at both ends against named bodies: its upper end a short distance above the outer boundary of the frame body, its lower end at the concave face of that carriage's jaw pad where the face meets the pipe, and the whole line stated to lie in the upper part of the view. The cutting plane itself is unchanged, so FIG. 3 and the description of FIG. 3 needed no edit.

FIG. 2: the drive face was drawn on the wrong segment because the brief itself hedged 'which segment carries it ... shown schematically', which left the renderer free to choose. The specification does not assign the drive face to either segment, so this is a depiction choice, not an invention fact, and I resolved it the way the brief already intended rather than the way the pixels came out. The brief now states positively that the ring drive face 36 lies on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint, and that the upper segment's outer boundary is circular throughout, and the leader entry repeats the segment. No specification text changed.

FIG. 3: the anchors for 20 and 34 collided because both were described against the same small region of the block, the hatching just above the opening and the open space just right of the post. I gave the two parts separated regions to sit in by stating that the opening lies in the lower portion of the block, which leaves a broad hatched region above it. 20 now targets that broad hatched region, and 34 targets the open unhatched space inside the opening right of the post end. The placement of the slot within the block's depth is not disclosed, so choosing the lower portion is a depiction convention needed to keep two labelled parts distinguishable, and nothing about it entered the specification or the claims.

FIG. 4: the reported artifacts were a closed slot outline under the handle near the pivot and a longitudinal seam line inside the lever. Rather than banning internal strokes, which the instructions forbid as a generic negative control, I described the handle positively: a plain elongated lever of constant width, two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from pivot to tip, a short straight end closing it, and the area between the edges plain. The phrase 'the handle mounting and its gap' in the schematic list was the likely source of the notch, so the housing opening is now described positively as the top and right walls stopping short of one another to leave an opening the lever passes through.

FIG. 6: the renderer transposed the stacking, drawing left and right bodies with a vertical gap. I kept the upper/lower arrangement rather than flipping the brief to match the pixels, because that arrangement follows FIG. 1, where the first frame half is the upper semicircular body and the second is the lower one, so at the latch-end joint the two ends are stacked vertically. The orientation is now stated three ways that reinforce each other: the circumferential direction runs vertically from top to bottom, the two bodies stand one above the other with a narrow horizontal gap across the middle, and each body ends at a straight horizontal end face, the upper ending downward and the lower ending upward.

Trimming was needed because every corrected brief crossed the 2800-character ceiling once the disambiguating geometry went in. I cut only hedges and redundancy, for example the duplicated 'shown schematically' qualifiers about pad depth, carriage apportionment, slot handedness, and spring seats, and never a body, contact, opening, or relationship that a sheet has to show. FIG. 5 was not touched: it passed and nothing in it depends on the five repairs.

Nothing in draft/ changed this turn. The five findings were all drawing findings, and each was fixable in the brief that governs the sheet, so the invention text stayed the authority above the briefs and the briefs stayed the authority above the pixels.

input.summary: Fixed the two reviewer findings, both confined to figure briefs. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 now describe the same geometry for oblique slot 34: a pocket formed in the ring and open at one axial face, which is what the FIG. 3 section shows and what the follower needs in order to enter from the guide mouth. FIG. 4's schematic list now designates the plain outline and constant width of the latch handle 50 as a depiction convention, so the lever silhouette reads as the generic outline a drawing has to pick rather than as an asserted shape. draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md were left shape-neutral and untouched, as were the claims and the numeral table. Two briefs crossed the 2800-character ceiling once the additions went in, so I trimmed a redundant hedge and a wordy phrase in FIG. 4; all six briefs are now under the limit, all 26 numerals are still carried, and no sheet's numeral list changed.
reasoning: The slot contradiction was resolved toward the blind pocket rather than the through opening because FIG. 3 is the axial section of that same feature and shows the follower post entering the slot from the groove mouth. A through slot would break out at both faces of the ring in that section, which the section does not show, and the disclosure says only that each carriage has 'a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring', so it constrains neither. Harmonizing on the geometry the section already needs keeps both briefs consistent without touching the specification, which stays neutral on whether the slot is blind or through.

FIG. 3's schematic list said 'the way the oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20', which presupposed the through geometry the section contradicts. It now says the slot 'is formed in' the ring, matching both the section body text and the corrected FIG. 2 wording.

For the latch handle, the fix belongs only in the schematic list. The positive description in the FIG. 4 body, the two unbroken long parallel edges and the plain area between them, is what stopped the spurious notch and internal seam line that failed this sheet last round, so I kept it intact and added the convention designation instead of weakening the geometry. The description and claims already say nothing about handle shape, so nothing there needed to change.

FIG. 4 had only 11 characters of headroom before the addition. I recovered space by dropping 'the gap between the two frame ends' from the schematic list, since the body already describes that gap positively as a narrow gap between the two frame bodies with the band ends meeting in it, and by shortening 'in the closed condition' to 'closed'. No body, contact, opening, or relationship was removed.

I left the on-disk reversions in FIG-2.md and FIG-3.md alone. The leader entries for the ring drive face 36, the segmented cam ring 20, and the oblique slot 34 are back to their shorter forms, but each brief's body text still places those parts unambiguously, the review confirmed the drive face sits on segment 24 in both FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, and no anchor-collision or endpoint finding was raised this round.

This turn touched only figure briefs and did not alter the Background's account of the problem the coupled cam ring and the force-limiting spring stack solve, which is the material any later argument would draw on. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the art in front of this draft may be incomplete.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so that the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints is shown schematically.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The region within the inner boundary is open, the ring being shown removed from the frame.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus and open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those positions are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary; that handedness is shown schematically.

The ring drive face 36 lies on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there the outer boundary runs for a short length as a straight surface slanting inward toward that joint. The outer boundary of the upper segment, the first cam ring segment 22, is circular throughout. The length of the slanting surface is shown schematically.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening through which it passes, the plain outline and constant width of the latch handle 50, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the two bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a short straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

The latch handle 50 is a plain elongated lever of constant width, its two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between those edges plain. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, and a short arm reaches from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls of the latch housing 58 stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.
